question: Given a continuous function \(f\) on \([a,b]\) and two tagged partitions \(P\) and \(Q\) with norms \(\eta_P\) and \(\eta_Q\), the lecture states that \(\lvert S_f(P)-S_f(Q)\rvert \le (\omega_f(\eta_P)+\omega_f(\eta_Q))(b-a)\). Explain why, as both norms tend to zero, the difference between the two Riemann sums tends to zero, and what this implies about the convergence of Riemann sums for \(f\).
answer: Because the modulus of continuity \(\omega_f(\eta)\) tends to zero as \(\eta\to0\), the bound \((\omega_f(\eta_P)+\omega_f(\eta_Q))(b-a)\) also tends to zero when both \(\eta_P\) and \(\eta_Q\) go to zero. Hence \(\lvert S_f(P)-S_f(Q)\rvert\to0\). This shows that any two sequences of Riemann sums whose partition norms approach zero must converge to the same limit, establishing the convergence of Riemann sums for \(f\).

question: The lecture gives the estimate \(\lvert S_f(P)-S_f(P')\rvert \le \omega_f(\lVert P\rVert)(b-a)\) when \(P'\) is a refinement of \(P\). Using this estimate and the fact that the norm of a refinement is strictly smaller, explain why the sequence of Riemann sums for a fixed continuous function \(f\) is Cauchy.
answer: For any \(\varepsilon>0\) choose \(\delta>0\) such that \(\omega_f(\delta)(b-a)<\varepsilon\). If \(P\) and \(P'\) are partitions with \(\lVert P\rVert,\lVert P'\rVert<\delta\), then \(\lvert S_f(P)-S_f(P')\rvert\le\omega_f(\lVert P\rVert)(b-a)<\varepsilon\). Thus the sequence of Riemann sums is Cauchy, because the difference between any two terms can be made arbitrarily small by taking partitions fine enough.

question: Consider two tagged partitions \((X, X_c)\) and \((Y, Y_c)\) of the same interval \([a,b]\).  Using the estimate that the absolute difference of their Riemann sums is bounded by the modulus of continuity evaluated at the coarser partition times the length of the interval, explain why refining a partition (i.e., decreasing its norm) necessarily reduces the difference between the corresponding Riemann sums.
answer: The bound \(\bigl|S(X,X_c)-S(Y,Y_c)\bigr|\le \omega_f(\|X\|)(b-a)\) shows that the difference is controlled by the modulus of continuity evaluated at the norm of the coarser partition.  Because \(\omega_f\) is increasing and \(\omega_f(\eta)\to0\) as \(\eta\to0\), decreasing the norm of a partition makes \(\omega_f(\|X\|)\) smaller, thereby shrinking the upper bound on the difference.  Hence refining a partition necessarily reduces the difference between the corresponding Riemann sums.

question: The lecture states that for every sequence of tagged partitions whose norms converge to zero, the corresponding Riemann sums converge to a common number, which is defined as the Riemann integral of the function.  Explain how the convergence of all such sequences leads to a well‑defined integral and why this limit is independent of the particular sequence chosen.
answer: For any two sequences of partitions \((X^n,X_c^n)\) and \((Y^m,Y_c^m)\) with \(\|X^n\|\to0\) and \(\|Y^m\|\to0\), the estimate \(\bigl|S(X^n,X_c^n)-S(Y^m,Y_c^m)\bigr|\le\omega_f(\max\{\|X^n\|,\|Y^m\|\})(b-a)\) shows that the difference between any two sums can be made arbitrarily small.  Therefore the limits of all such sequences must coincide.  This uniqueness of the limit justifies defining the Riemann integral as that common value, independent of the particular sequence of partitions chosen.

question: Let \(f\) and \(g\) be continuous functions on \([a,b]\) and let \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\). Using the linearity of Riemann sums and the comparison theorem for partitions, show that the Riemann sum of \(\alpha f+g\) over any tagged partition converges to \(\alpha\int_a^b f + \int_a^b g\).
answer: The Riemann sum is linear in the function: \(S(\alpha f+g,P)=\alpha S(f,P)+S(g,P)\). For any \(\varepsilon>0\) choose a partition \(P\) fine enough that \(|S(f,P)-\int_a^b f|<\varepsilon/(2(|\alpha|+1))\) and \(|S(g,P)-\int_a^b g|<\varepsilon/(2(|\alpha|+1))\). Then \(|S(\alpha f+g,P)-(\alpha\int_a^b f+\int_a^b g)|\le |\alpha||S(f,P)-\int_a^b f|+|S(g,P)-\int_a^b g|<\varepsilon\). Hence the Riemann sums of \(\alpha f+g\) converge to \(\alpha\int_a^b f+\int_a^b g\).

question: Suppose \(X\) and \(Y\) are tagged partitions of \([a,b]\) with \(X\subseteq Y\). For a continuous function \(f\), explain how the comparison theorem implies that the Riemann sum over \(Y\) is a better approximation to the integral than the sum over \(X\), and quantify the difference in terms of the mesh size.
answer: The comparison theorem states that if \(X\subseteq Y\), then for any choice of tags \(S(f,X)\le S(f,Y)\le U(f,Y)\le U(f,X)\). Since \(f\) is continuous, the difference \(U(f,X)-L(f,X)\) tends to zero as the mesh \(\|X\|\) tends to zero. Therefore \(|S(f,Y)-S(f,X)|\le U(f,X)-L(f,X)\). For a given \(\varepsilon>0\) we can choose a partition \(X\) with mesh \(\|X\|<\delta\) such that \(U(f,X)-L(f,X)<\varepsilon\); then any refinement \(Y\) will satisfy \(|S(f,Y)-S(f,X)|<\varepsilon\). Thus the Riemann sum over the finer partition \(Y\) is a closer approximation to the integral than that over \(X\).

question: Explain why, for the linear function \(f(x)=ax+b\), the modulus of continuity \(\omega_f(\eta)\) equals \(|a|\eta\), using the definition \(\omega_f(\eta)=\sup\{|f(x)-f(y)|:|x-y|\le\eta\}\).
answer: For \(f(x)=ax+b\) we have \(|f(x)-f(y)|=|a||x-y|\). Since \(|x-y|\le\eta\), it follows that \(|f(x)-f(y)|\le |a|\eta\). The supremum of the set of all such values is therefore \(|a|\eta\), and this value is achieved when \(|x-y|=\eta\). Hence \(\omega_f(\eta)=|a|\eta\).

question: Given that the modulus of continuity is defined as a supremum over all \(|f(x)-f(y)|\) with \(|x-y|\le\eta\), justify why the property \(\omega_f(\eta)\to0\) as \(\eta\to0\) follows from the definition of continuity of \(f\).
answer: The modulus \(\omega_f(\eta)\) is the least upper bound of the set \(\{|f(x)-f(y)|:|x-y|\le\eta\}\).  Continuity of \(f\) at every point means that for any \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a \(\delta>0\) such that \(|x-y|<\delta\) implies \(|f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon\).  Therefore, when \(\eta<\delta\), every element of the set is less than \(\varepsilon\), so its supremum \(\omega_f(\eta)\) is also less than \(\varepsilon\).  As \(\varepsilon\) was arbitrary, this shows \(\omega_f(\eta)\to0\) as \(\eta\to0\).

question: In the discussion of the Riemann integral as a linear operator, how does its action on continuous functions—viewed as morphisms between topological spaces—illustrate the preservation of additive structure across these categories?

Since continuous functions are morphisms, this property shows that the integral preserves the additive composition of morphisms: the image of a sum of morphisms is the sum of their images. Thus, the integral acts as a functor that respects the additive structure inherent in the category of continuous functions.
